concept.body: A rectangle is a parallelogram with a right angle — supplementary consecutive angles then force all four corners to 90°. It keeps every parallelogram property (opposite sides congruent, diagonals bisect each other) and adds ONE new one: the diagonals are congruent. So the intersection point is equidistant from all four vertices.

explanationVariants: Diagonals bisecting each other is the ch2 parallelogram property — inherited, not new. The rectangle's new fact is AC = BD.
Bisection: every parallelogram. Congruence of diagonals: rectangles.

widget.prompt: Diagonals that bisect each other: parallelogram property or rectangle upgrade?

options.label: Parallelogram property — every parallelogram's diagonals bisect each other
options.feedback: Proved in ch2 for ALL parallelograms. The rectangle's addition is congruent diagonals.

options.label: Rectangle upgrade — only rectangles bisect
options.feedback: Bisection is universal among parallelograms (ch2's four-triangle ASA proof). Rectangles add CONGRUENT diagonals.

options.label: Square-only property
options.feedback: Squares inherit it too, but so does every leaning parallelogram — bisection is the family-wide rule.

options.label: True for every quadrilateral
options.feedback: A kite's diagonals, for one, don't bisect each other both ways. Bisection belongs to parallelograms.

steps.body: A **rectangle** is a parallelogram with one right angle — and that's all you must ASK for. Consecutive angles of a parallelogram are supplementary, so one 90° forces its neighbors to 90°, and theirs in turn: all four square up from a single corner. Cheap definition, rich consequences.
Drag the corner. The shape names itself.

widget.prompt: Three corners are pinned at (0,0), (6,0) and (6,4). Place the fourth so the shape is a rectangle.
widget.successFeedback: (0, 4). Sides 6, 4, 6, 4 — and the two diagonals come out EQUAL, which is exactly what separates a rectangle from an ordinary parallelogram. Drag the corner around and watch the name change underneath: the shape tells you what it is, and the hierarchy stops being a list to recite.
widget.sideFeedback: Your corner is not above A, so the side from C to it cannot match AB. Watch the four lengths in the readout: a rectangle's opposite sides must pair up, 6 with 6 and 4 with 4.
widget.angleFeedback: Your corner is in the right column now, so one pair of sides matches — but the height is wrong, so the last side does not match CB and the diagonals come out unequal. Read the name underneath: it is not the one you were asked for.

predict.prompt: When the fourth vertex reaches the rectangle position, which extra property appears beyond opposite sides matching?
predict.reveal: A rectangle is a parallelogram with right angles; its diagonals are both bisected and congruent. If all four sides had gone equal you'd have the rhombus instead — the classic mixup: a rhombus matches its sides but its diagonals are generally NOT congruent. And 'only one diagonal bisected' can't happen here at all: in any parallelogram the diagonals bisect each other.

cml.actionGoal: Move one vertex and coordinate side lengths, diagonals, angles, and family classification.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: Move the corner horizontally while preserving one pair of opposite sides. Which rectangle property fails first?

explanation.prompt: What evidence distinguishes the rectangle from a generic parallelogram here?

options.label: Its diagonals are congruent in addition to bisecting each other.
options.feedback: That extra invariant is characteristic of rectangles.

options.label: Its sides are drawn horizontally and vertically.
options.feedback: Orientation is irrelevant; a rotated rectangle is still a rectangle.

options.label: Its longer side is exactly 6 units.
options.feedback: Specific dimensions do not define the family.

steps.body: Rectangles add exactly one new tool to the parallelogram kit: **the diagonals are congruent.** (They still bisect each other — that's inherited.) Congruent + bisecting means all four half-diagonals are equal: the intersection point sits at the same distance from every corner.

explanationVariants: Congruent diagonals cut by mutual bisection: 2x + 1 = x + 9 gives x = 8, so each half is 17 and the full diagonal is 34.
Set the two half-diagonals equal (rectangle!), solve, then double: 17 × 2 = 34.

widget.prompt: In rectangle ABCD the diagonals meet at O, with AO = 2x + 1 and BO = x + 9. Find the FULL diagonal AC.

commonErrors.feedback: 8 is x itself — the problem asks for the diagonal. AO = 2(8) + 1 = 17, and AC doubles it: 34.
17 is the HALF-diagonal AO. Diagonals bisect each other, so AC = 2 × 17 = 34.
26 = 17 + 9 mixes a half-diagonal with x + a stray 9 — recompute: BO = 8 + 9 = 17 too, and AC = 34.

explanationVariants: Bisecting diagonals come free with EVERY parallelogram; congruent diagonals are the rectangle's upgrade.
AO = OC is old news (ch2); AC = BD is the new rectangle-only fact.

widget.prompt: In rectangle ABCD with diagonals meeting at O, which statement is true because it's a RECTANGLE (not just a parallelogram)?

options.label: AC = BD
options.feedback: Congruent diagonals are the rectangle's signature — a generic parallelogram's diagonals differ in length.

options.label: AO = OC
options.feedback: That's mutual bisection — every parallelogram does it (ch2). The rectangle's new gift is AC = BD.

options.label: AB = DC
options.feedback: Opposite sides congruent is the ch2 parallelogram property — no right angle needed. The upgrade is AC = BD.

options.label: AB ∥ DC
options.feedback: Parallel opposite sides is the parallelogram DEFINITION itself. The rectangle adds congruent diagonals: AC = BD.

steps.body: The right angles also invite the Pythagorean theorem in: a rectangle's diagonal is the hypotenuse of a right triangle whose legs are the two side lengths. Width 9, length 12: diagonal = √(9² + 12²) = √225 = 15 — the 3-4-5 family scaled by 3, exactly as in the trig course.

explanationVariants: The sides are the legs of a right triangle whose hypotenuse is the diagonal: 15.

widget.prompt: A rectangle measures 9 by 12. How long is each diagonal?

commonErrors.feedback: 21 = 9 + 12 adds side lengths — Pythagoras adds their SQUARES: √(81 + 144) = 15.
10.5 = (9 + 12)/2 averages the sides — the diagonal is a hypotenuse, not a mean: 15.
7.94 ≈ √(144 − 81) subtracts squares, which finds a missing LEG. Both sides are legs here: add → 15.

widget.prompt: Same 9-by-12 rectangle. How far is the diagonals' intersection point from each corner?

commonErrors.feedback: 15 is the FULL diagonal. The intersection bisects it, so each corner sits half that away: 7.5.
5.25 = 10.5/2 halves the wrong number (the side average). Half the true diagonal: 15/2 = 7.5.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Half of the 15 diagonal: 7.5 — the same for all four corners, since the diagonals are congruent AND bisect each other.

hints: A carpenter checks a doorframe by measuring both diagonals — what property is being tested?
A parallelogram-shaped (leaning) frame still has bisecting diagonals — but NOT congruent ones.
Equal diagonals in a parallelogram frame certify right angles.
explanationVariants: Equal diagonals are exclusive to rectangles among parallelograms — matching tape measures certify the frame is square-cornered.
A leaning frame's diagonals split into a long one and a short one; equality returns only at 90°.

widget.prompt: A carpenter measures a doorframe's two diagonals and finds them equal (the frame's opposite sides are already equal). What's certified?

options.label: The frame is a true rectangle — right angles guaranteed
options.feedback: Equal opposite sides make it a parallelogram; equal diagonals upgrade a parallelogram to a rectangle. Doors that close properly depend on it.

options.label: Only that the frame is a parallelogram
options.feedback: Parallelogram-ness was already given by the equal opposite sides — the equal DIAGONALS add the rectangle upgrade.

options.label: The frame is a square
options.feedback: Squares also need all four SIDES equal — a doorframe is usually taller than wide. Equal diagonals certify rectangle, no more.

options.label: Nothing — all quadrilaterals have equal diagonals
options.feedback: Most don't: lean the frame and one diagonal stretches while the other shrinks. Equality is the rectangle's tell.

takeaways: Rectangle = parallelogram + one right angle; supplements spread it to all four.
New property: congruent diagonals (bisection is inherited) — all four half-diagonals equal.
The diagonal is a hypotenuse: √(w² + ℓ²), Pythagoras style.
steps.teaser: Next: equal sides instead of equal angles — the rhombus and its perpendicular diagonals.
